articles.title: Jeremy Latcham takes over as new DC Studios chief: three ways this could play out for the DC universe
articles.author: Roman Pavlyuchenko, Lecturer in Marketing, University of Bath
paras: Hollywood’s superhero industrial complex revolves around DC and Marvel, two huge studios that style themselves as “cinematic universes”. DC owns characters like Batman, Superman and Wonder Woman, while Marvel owns Spider-Man, Captain America and X-Men among others. Problems have been plaguing both studios in recent years, but DC more so.

In April 2026, I wrote that DC Studios president James Gunn was one of the key risk factors for the DC cinematic universe. Building an entire universe around his unique creative vision alone, I argued, could pose serious problems for DC.

The news that Gunn is out as the head of DC Studios after four years seems to have confirmed my hunch. While the director will continue working on the Superman sequel and other films and series slated for 2027, he is being replaced by one-time Marvel veteran Jeremy Latcham.

With such a seismic shift in leadership – and following the huge 2026 box-office flops of Supergirl and Clayface (the horror take on the superhero genre) – what can viewers expect from the DC Cinematic Universe in the coming months and years? Based on my ongoing research into superhero franchises, I see several possible scenarios that could shape the Hollywood studio.
1. Different management, same direction

Gunn is chiefly a director, famous for his quirky action pieces littered with witty dialogue and a penchant for 1980s pop music. Marvel’s Guardians of the Galaxy trilogy (2014-2023) is undoubtedly the best entry into this body of work – films he made before taking on the DC job.

His replacement, Jeremy Latcham, is a producer. One of the earliest employees of Marvel Studios, Latcham helped propel the Marvel cinematic universe to global acclaim with production credits on Iron Man (2008) and The Avengers (2012).
To have a producer and not a director in charge brings in a different skill set to the job, including a certain level of operational excellence required to oversee a cinematic universe.

At the same time, a potential improvement in operational excellence does not address the underlying issues currently affecting the DC universe. For instance, no major villain or narrative direction has been introduced in the new DC Cinematic Universe. Operational excellence is no guarantee of creative and commercial success.
As a complex narrative that would take years to reach a proper dramatic resolution, the DC cinematic universe is currently in disarray.

While 2025’s Superman took viewers into known territory, the other staples of DC comics like Batman, Wonder Woman, or Aquaman are nowhere to be seen. Indeed, no release dates for films about any of these heroes have been confirmed yet. This comes amid one DC project after another being cancelled.

Crucially, the shows and films that have been released do not seem to speak well to one another or the broader DC world. For instance, Clayface, DC’s most recent film makes no direct references to Batman or Superman. It doesn’t even have a post-credits scene – a staple of a good superhero film that sets the scene for what comes next and allows fans to speculate.
In this challenging climate, Latcham’s role may be to clean house and ensure that incoming projects let fans see the DC cinematic universe as a holistic whole worthy of years-long commitment.

It is unlikely that the cancelled projects will be revived. It’s also too late to fix the earlier problems. So Latcham will have to unite and interconnect the projects still on the slate. This seems the most likely scenario.

The “nuclear option” for any expansive narrative is a hard reset, where the existing continuity is brushed aside and a new story universe is created. This is not without precedent in comics, and DC’s recent pivot from their original cinematic universe (2013-2023) proves that the move itself is feasible.

This might also make sense because a new creative direction in an otherwise established continuity may cause more problems than it fixes. Famously, in the previous DC cinematic universe (2013-2023), director Joss Whedon replaced Zack Snyder at the helm of 2017’s Justice League in the middle of post-production.
The switch resulted in a tonally inconsistent film that split the fanbase, forcing DC to release a standalone “Snyder Cut” a few years later.
At the same time, a hard reset may cause a PR crisis given how close it is to the previous reset, which only took place last year when Gunn’s Superman was released.

A proper reset also requires careful thinking about what actually happens afterwards. Here, it appears that the decision to oust Gunn is a fresh one, leaving Latcham little time to figure out major reinventions.

Less than 24 hours after Gunn’s departure, there were already reports that the new management was thinking of rebooting the DC universe again. So while this radical option is an increasing possibility, some serious thinking around long-term planning is required.
Whatever direction DC takes, one thing is clear: replacing Gunn with Latcham is not merely a change in leadership, but potentially a change in how DC thinks about its cinematic universe.

articles.title: How the discovery of a Roman fort rekindled interest in an emperor immortalised in Welsh mythology
articles.author: Aled Ll Jones, Head of School & Reader in Welsh & Medieval Literature, Bangor University
paras: The recent discovery of a Roman timber fort in the Preseli hills of Pembrokeshire, south-west Wales, has brought a medieval Welsh legend into fresh focus.

The site is mentioned in Breuddwyd Macsen Wledig (The Dream of Macsen Wledig), a story about a Roman emperor who travels to Wales. Until now, the account of a camp in that location had largely been treated as a product of medieval imagination. But the archaeological discovery raises an intriguing question: can ancient stories preserve memories of places and events that have been lost to history?

The Dream of Macsen Wledig is one of the 11 medieval Welsh-language tales traditionally grouped together as the Mabinogion. These tales blend history, folklore, magic and legend, while some people see in them lost myths. Featuring kings, warriors, magicians and supernatural beings, the stories offer a glimpse into how people in medieval Wales understood their past and the world around them.

The tales survive in two important Welsh-language manuscripts. First, in Llyfr Gwyn Rhydderch (the White Book of Rhydderch), compiled around the mid-14th century, and second in Llyfr Coch Hergest (the Red Book of Hergest), written towards the end of that century.
But the stories themselves are older. They had been transmitted and copied since before King Edward I’s conquest of Wales in 1282, and perhaps as early as the 11th century.

Five of the tales feature Arthur, the legendary warrior whose tales spread throughout all of Europe. The Four Branches of the Mabinogi, are a group of stories spanning the landscapes of Wales, Ireland and England, of this world and the supernatural otherworld. The remaining two, including The Dream of Macsen Wledig, reshape particular strands of early British history through native storytelling. All the tales offer imaginative accounts of power and political authority.
A Roman emperor in Welsh legend

In The Dream of Macsen Wledig, a Roman emperor falls in love with a woman he sees in a dream. Determined to find her, he sends messengers to follow the route he has dreamt. Their journey takes them across Europe and eventually to what is now Caernarfon, in north-west Wales.

The emperor is called Macsen Wledig (Macsen the Leader). His character is a literary composite of a number of historical characters, most notably the Galician Magnus Maximus, a Roman general who became Emperor in the late 4th century. Born in a province that is now part of Spain and Portugal, Magnus Maximus seized power in Britain and went on to rule much of the western Roman empire, including Gaul (roughly modern France and neighbouring regions).

His legacy in Wales is particularly significant. In the popular Welsh song Yma o Hyd (Still Here), first released in 1983, the singer and former politician Dafydd Iwan invokes Magnus Maximus’ departure from Britain, supposedly leaving Wales behind as an entire nation.
The song draws on a powerful literary tradition – that the departure of Rome from Britain, just before the arrival of the English, saw the birth of Welsh identity.

But the medieval story is not a straightforward account of historical events. Like the song, it blends historical memory with imagination. Its importance lies not simply in whether every detail is factually accurate, but in what the story tells us about how Welsh people understood the past.

The woman in Macsen’s dream is Elen Luyddog (Elen of the Hosts). She is also a composite character, associated with two figures named Helen or Helena – Helen of Caernarfon and Helena of Constantinople, mother of Constantine the Great. Both were 4th century saints.

In the story, Elen insists that Macsen travel to Wales to marry her. He agrees and she becomes empress. Her father is appointed Viceroy of Britain, and together they begin building powerful fortresses. Elen asks Macsen to establish three towns: Caerllion (Caerleon), Caerfyrddin (Carmarthen) and Caernarfon.

She also asks him to build roads to link them. Sarn Elen (Elen’s Way) is still the name given to the main Roman road complex linking north and south Wales. The story offers a legendary explanation for features of the landscape that people could still see around them centuries later.
Ancient words, modern truths

One passage in particular in the tale has taken on new significance following the archaeological discovery at Y Frenni Fawr hill in Pembrokeshire. Specifically, the moment in the tale which describes Macsen travelling from Carmarthen to the summit of the hill to hunt. There, he establishes a camp known as Cadair Facsen, or Macsen’s Chair.

Until recently, this reference was generally understood as part of the story’s imaginative landscape. But the discovery of a Roman timber fort on the hill, alongside coins dating from the period of the historical Magnus Maximus, offers a fascinating connection between the medieval account and the archaeological record.

It does not mean that every detail of the story is historically true, but it does suggest that the people who told and recorded the tale may have known about real places and features of the landscape that have since been forgotten. It also raises the possibility that other details in medieval Welsh stories could preserve valuable historical information.

The discovery at Y Frenni Fawr reminds us that the past is not always neatly divided between history and legend. Medieval stories preserve important pieces of older knowledge, even when they have been reshaped over generations. By reading them along with archaeology, linguistics and an eye to the landscape itself, we may discover more about the people who once lived in Wales, the stories they told and how they understood their place in the world. By doing this we understand more about the world we live in today.

articles.title: Fjord turns a Norwegian child protection battle into a chilling moral thriller
articles.author: Caroline Oliver, Professor of Sociology, UCL
paras: Over the summer I took respite from the UK heat in the Norwegian fjords. So I was pleased to revisit that dramatic landscape through director Christian Mungiu’s new film, Fjord. Norway provides the backdrop to his story of an incomer family fighting for the right to keep their children amid accusations of mistreatment.

The film opens with the musical strains of the hymn Amazing Grace. The song hints at both the long-held traditional values of Norway’s religious past, and the key battleground of belief and cultural values in the drama to come.

From there, the film pushes into a tangle of competing loyalties and sympathies. As the characters’ allegiances shift, the audience is forced to constantly reexamine their own values. Ultimately, the fractures of the dramatic landscape mirror the complex human relationships carved out within it.

The tale begins with the arrival of the Gheorghius family. Romanian Mihai (an unrecognisable Sebastian Stan) and Norwegian Lisbet (Renate Reinsve) move into the small community of Lisbet’s birth with their children. They live next door to amiable headteacher Mats (Markus Tønseth) and his family. Here, everyone knows everyone. The Gheorghius seem likeable, but they are viewed warily as they express their Christian evangelical faith through mundane acts. Welcome quickly turns to suspicion and then escalates to accusation as one of the children, Elia, arrives at school with bruises.
The remainder of the film provides an emotionally harrowing account of the interaction of the state and personal life as the children are removed from their parent’s care.

Through tense encounters with the police, schools and social welfare services, the film tackles cultural and moral divides in all their forms. It explores discipline and abuse, religious dogma, gender roles, sexuality and the clash between progressive ideals and conservative faith.

Fjord questions where lines should be drawn when navigating conflicting values, highlighting the dangers of weaponising difference. These themes speak directly to long-standing concerns in my own field as an anthropologist and sociologist of migration. This work examines how newcomers are routinely cast as “other”, asking instead how we can live together with and across our differences.

Fjord asks unsettling questions about power: whose responsibility is it to safeguard rights? And precisely whose rights take precedence? The rights of children to be protected, the right of parents to a family and religious life of their choosing, or the demand of wider society not to be offended?

Mungiu artfully compels viewers to vacillate between being drawn to and then repelled by both the family and state’s actions. The Gheorghius children have no power to challenge abuse, whether physical, through slaps, or mental through religious indoctrination. Here, the universal (western) values of human and child rights trump the localised, religious, conservative values of the incomers.

Yet the Norwegian state is not depicted as a pure saviour: its representatives are icy, detached and bureaucratic in their engagement with the family. The state expects “assimilation” and rejects the family’s old-fashioned parenting beliefs, uncomfortably echoing its historical policies of erasing Sámi language and culture under Norway’s project of nationalism and cultural homogeneity. Words are put in the mouths of the newcomers. We see language twisted and the parents’ limited understanding of rights misused.

Meanwhile “modern” values around liberal parenting and care for older people are exposed. Teenage Noora, scrolling screens in her bedroom, is sad, anxious and hiding her self-harm. And Mat’s ageing, disabled father does not fare much better.

While a story of fissures, Fjord examines bonds too, across family, peers, lovers and community. Mia (Lisa Carlehed) feels like a breath of fresh air as she gains sympathy for the family, resuming the career she stepped down for caring reasons, by representing them as their defence lawyer.

Mingui skilfully exploits the empathy of his viewers based on their own personal values and experiences. As a mother myself, I felt visceral pain as Lisbet, unable to breastfeed her youngest child, struggles to express her milk under the stress of separation.

Yet some of the bonds that Mingui explores – of religion and motherhood – are also questioned. The community’s quiet, religious nature is quickly reframed as cronyism. At the same time, it is uncomfortable to watch Mihai exploit the family’s hardship by rallying media-savvy, conservative Christian networks across Romania and the United States. Motherhood itself is also weaponised, with the welfare officer’s childlessness dragged into the child protection hearing to undermine her competence and authority.

Although some critics have argued that the film relies on caricatures of child protection services, it actually critiques that exact mindset: the cartoonish binaries, the political weaponisation and the urge to jump to easy conclusions.

Instead of tidy resolution, the film offers only mounting ambiguity. Fjord closes on a deliberate, painfully quiet anti-climax. It’s a reminder that when clashing worldviews scream across a void, nobody wins.

articles.title: BBC documentary takes eight children on a nature field trip to explore eco-anxiety
articles.author: Michael Joseph Richardson, Senior Lecturer in Human Geography, Newcastle University
paras: A dawn chorus begins with the chirping and tweeting of birds, wind blowing through the trees and a woodpecker hammering on wood. Dappled sunlight bursts through the forest canopy, and an evocative choir of children join the birds in song:

We will stand up tall in the shadow of your power. For every empty promise, we will shout it even louder. No more sacrifice or compromise for profits, greed and lies. It’s time to build the future; Don’t ignore the children’s cries.

This powerful opening to Climate Change and Me: Future Council, an environmental documentary currently showing on the BBC, quickly shifts to a lighter tone. After running over mossy undergrowth through the forest, the children respond cheekily to the director’s call for another take.

Play can open up different learning and communication styles, particularly for younger children. This is something Australian director Damon Gameau taps into throughout the one-hour programme as he leads a fieldtrip around Europe. Eight climate-conscious children, selected from over 1,000 applicants aged nine to 16, travel together on the “Bumblebus” – a yellow American-style schoolbus, powered by biofuel – in pursuit of a brighter, greener future.

Aspects of this programme remind me of my own research. I work as a storyteller on a project called Birds, Bees, Bikes and Trees. Our team’s work is wide-ranging. Over the past three years, I have worked with a group of 20 young fathers to explore the everyday environmental actions they can (and often do) take. I have also led sessions in classrooms exploring urban relationships to nature through science and storytelling with more than 300 schoolchildren. Our design of these activities is shaped by care and curiosity, not anger or anxiety.

I am drawn particularly to the BBC programme’s use of magical realism. This artistic style of storytelling is similar to a novum within science fiction – a literary device such as time travel that distorts reality. In making both the familiar strange and the mythical mundane, it can open our imagination to new possibilities. I use this approach in my own work.

Don’t Look Down, for example is an upcoming children’s storybook I have created with primary schoolchildren in Newcastle and with Atomhawk, a video game art studio. Their illustrations convey an imaginary world abandoned by adults in a relentless pursuit of growth and innovation. Through this alternative future, a child can begin to ask questions of the world in which they live, and the stories they have been told about how to care for it.

Back to the TV screen, and Gameau’s show features several scenes where some of the eight children are led to tears. There is sadness, anger and frustration. Some say they feel overwhelmed by pressure to make the planet a better place and fix a world which they did not break.

By Lake Geneva, the children meet with climate activist Clover Hogan to offload some of their strong feelings. Hogan is also an eco-anxiety researcher. In 2019, she founded a youth-driven not-for-profit organisation called Force of Nature which brings young people into conversations with decision-makers. She explains to the children that their anxiety is a healthy response and shows that they care. Hogan says: “When we feel that sadness, when we feel that anger, when we feel that frustration, that is the internal alarm bell that tells us something is really, really wrong.”
The show advocates for involving children and young people in decision-making. This is both an admirable and achievable mission.

At the Nestlé corporation headquarters in Switzerland, the children meet with the global head of public affairs for this food and drink multinational. They press him hard on Nestlé’s lack of climate action and on the firm’s excessive use of single-use plastic packaging. They called out “empty words and empty promises” and one challenged him with damning words: “You are not a powerful leader, you are a disgrace.”

The film depicts the children’s anger as righteous. There is evidence to suggest that eco-anger is a more productive emotion than eco-anxiety. But there is a risk that young’s people activism plays into the trope of powerful elites, if too narrowly defined by either anxiety or anger.

While both are key features of this programme, recent research identifies a wider range of responses to climate change. In doing so, the researchers encourage expanding our vocabulary on climate change and how we experience it, to avoid overly reductive responses to this environmental crisis.

Informed by my own research, I had hoped to see more reflection on the transformative potential of nature for mental health benefits. Children should not be defined as being without hope, power or influence but nor should nature.

Young people can claim their agency and be encouraged to actively build their green future, as my project will be doing at a green jobs career event for young people. That green future could involve the representation of younger generations on the boards of big companies, but it might also involve community power or nature-positive regeneration projects. The choice could be theirs.

articles.title: Rivals season two: why a shocking death in episode six changes everything for the women of Rutshire
articles.author: Claudine van Hensbergen, Associate Professor, Eighteenth-Century English Literature, Northumbria University, Newcastle
paras: Warning: this article contains spoilers for Rivals season two part one.
There was something masterful about the episode six cliffhanger of Rivals’ season two, based on Jilly Cooper’s much-loved novel. It was certainly ambitious in scope.

There was the exposure of the affair between Tony Baddingham (David Tennant) and Maud O'Hara (Victoria Smurfit), wife of his nemesis Declan O'Hara (Aidan Turner). Then there was Maud and Declan’s teenage daughter Caitlin (Catriona Chandler) losing her virginity to Tony’s teenage son, Archie (Louis Landau). And Cameron Cook (Nafessa Williams) finally realising that her lover Rupert Campbell-Black (Alex Hassell) is in love with eldest O'Hara daughter Taggie (Bella Mclean), and Lizzie Vereker (Katherine Parkinson) resuming her affair with tech millionaire Freddie Jones (Danny Dyer). All against a backdrop of a dramatic storm.
I admit I groaned inwardly at the use of the storm as a device, believing it would surely descend into terrible cliche. Instead, Rivals’ mid-season finale did something extraordinary.

In 60 minutes of high-drama television, the storm became both metaphor and agent, felling Tony’s beleaguered wife Monica (Claire Rushbrook) by its end, and weaving the threads of the narrative into the next – and what promises to be very different – act in the final six episodes of the season starting on November 11.

Early in the episode, the teenage Caitlin and Archie finally get together after Archie has been developing photos of wild birds, captured on his dad Tony’s camera. It seems their parents have not been careful with their own relationship. The teenagers find a photo of Maud – Caitlin’s mother – posing naked, with Tony’s voyeuristic reflection caught in a mirror. At this moment, Monica returns home.

Thankfully, the episode does not spend the rest of the hour teasing us over whether Monica will discover the photo. She sees it quickly, burns it in the fireplace, confronts Tony (who has now returned home) and walks out into the storm. And this is where things get interesting.
Rivals as a domestic tragedy

Monica’s walk through the storm is a King Lear-like moment. Exposure to the elements and a descent into frenzied madness bring reason into focus. She arrives on Lizzie’s doorstop and the two sit down to a cup of tea. Then brandy.

With this scene, the show examines the symmetry of their lives. And the two frumpiest and most downtrodden women in Jilly Cooper’s Rutshire become the beating heart of the episode – perhaps the whole series.
With this move, the TV show deviates dramatically from Cooper’s source material.

Suddenly liberated from the polite social conventions she has found smothering, Monica asks Lizzie about her affair with Freddie. Reeling from the revelation of Tony’s most calculated piece of adultery to date, Monica doesn’t ask Lizzie this to judge, but rather to encourage her to pursue love and happiness regardless of the damage it may cause to others.

The women’s conversation at the kitchen table lays bare the devastation wrought on their lives through their unswerving sense of duty. And to the demands of placing the needs of their husbands, and everyone else, first. It’s a crystallising moment where they see themselves properly for the first time, speaking honestly with each other.

Monica and Lizzie now agree they wouldn’t want their own daughters to live similar lives, and with this dawning realisation the viewer knows that the real moment of women’s liberation has just happened within the series.
Honesty and women’s writing

This call for honesty in human relationships feels like a connecting thread across so much writing by women. It can be found even in the work of the first professional woman writer, Aphra Behn (1640-1689). Behn’s popular novels, plays and poems explored many of the same social settings and concerns that we find in Cooper’s Rutshire: desire, marriage, money, fame, politics, love, power.

The world of Behn’s writing is that of Restoration England’s “merry monarch” Charles II, notorious for its sex, scandal and celebrity. Behn is fascinated by this social orbit – just as readers and viewers today are captivated by Cooper’s Rutshire. And yet her aim, as with the current TV adaptation, is ultimately to challenge the validity of that glossy world.

Because, in the very process of enjoying its sheer escapism, there is a sadness in both Cooper’s Rutshire and Behn’s Restoration London. This is not a world in which women can honestly be themselves, or pursue their own desires. With the second half of season two, Rivals now seems poised to offer us a perspective of a woman – Lizzie – who might achieve this rare feat.

It’s not the talented, couture-clad Cameron, a television producer poached from the US, who is the true trailblazer of the show. Rather, it’s Lizzie and Monica, in this quiet chat among the chintz and domesticity of the kitchen, who are about to turn the world of Rutshire on its head.

Monica is the catalyst for this moment of self-examination, but it is Lizzie who will reap the rewards. For by the end of the night, Monica is dead, killed when her car is crushed by a falling tree in the wild tempestuous weather.

Again, this is a notable deviation from Cooper’s novel. Cooper gives Monica her eventual rewards for bearing with Tony for so long. In her 2007 novel, Appassionata, we discover that she has divorced Tony and is now living happily in an open relationship with childhood friend Dame Enid Spink.

Women are at the heart of Rivals. The novel and TV show are set in the beautiful honey-coloured mansions of the Cotswolds, inhabited by svelte, beautiful, talented people who spend their lives flitting between the TV studio, the polo club and dinner parties. A triumvirate of imposing men run things – Tony Baddingham, Declan O'Hara and Rupert Campbell-Black – oozing sex appeal, power and machismo.

Yet with the cliffhanger episode, the TV series made clear its commitment to a much wider society beyond the screen. For it makes two quiet housewives its heroines. Where the tragic stage of the immediate moment belongs to Monica, the future belongs to Lizzie. And storm clouds, it seems, are gathering once more.

articles.title: As the UN adopts an equal world map, meet the three geographers who disputed how the Earth was charted 2000 years ago
articles.author: Daniel Hanigan, Junior Research Fellow in Classics at Trinity College, University of Cambridge
paras: For more than 200 years, the standard map of the world has been based on a 1569 chart of the globe pioneered by Flemish geographer Gerardus Mercator (1512–1594).

But in spite of its historic popularity, the Mercator Projection the has long been recognised as problematic. The main issue is that, for navigational reasons, it artificially enlarges the regions nearest to the poles, making Africa – which straddles the equator – appear roughly the same size as Greenland, despite being about 14 times larger.

On 4 September 2026, the UN passed a motion tabled by representatives from Togo and backed by a number of African nations, to endorse and adopt a new world map. The map in question is the Equal Earth Projection, developed in 2018 by prominent cartographers Bojan Šavrič, Tom Patterson and Bernhard Jenny.

It will, in theory, replace the Mercator Projection, which the Togo campaigners say risks insinuating that Africa and its peoples are politically and culturally peripheral. The Equal Earth Projection corrects this distortion by accurately depicting the relative areas of the continents.
This critique of Mercator is timely and important, and it also taps into a long history of disputes about how the continents should appear on the map.

Their sizes, and the politics of their representation, were already major points of contention for the ancient geographers of Greece and Rome, including Herodotus, Strabo and Pliny (the Elder), and each approached the depiction of the planet from a different perspective.
1. Herodotus on the symmetrical Earth

One of the earliest recorded attempts to correct the map comes from the fourth book of Herodotus’ Histories (5th century BCE). In it, the Greek geographer and historian mocks the work of earlier cartographers and accuses them of making their maps artificially symmetrical:

I laugh when I see that, though many before this have drawn maps of the Earth, yet no one has set the matter forth in an intelligent way; seeing that they draw Ocean flowing round the Earth, which is circular exactly as if drawn with compasses, and they make Asia equal in size to Europe.
Herodotus replaces this world picture with a strikingly different vision of the Earth in which Europe dwarfs both Asia and Libya (the name he uses to refer to Africa):

I wonder then at those who have parted off and divided the world into Libya, Asia and Europe, since the difference between these is not small; for in length Europe extends along by both, while in breadth it is clear to me that it is beyond comparison larger.
2. Strabo on scale and power

Herodotus gives no overall measurements of Libya (Africa). He describes it as very broad, connected to Asia, and smaller than Europe. The Greek geographer Strabo, writing under Roman rule (1st century BC), offers a different assessment. In the 17th book of his Geography, he challenges the conventional threefold continental division on the grounds that Libya falls far short of a third of the inhabited world and may in fact be smaller than Europe:

Now the writers who have divided the inhabited world according to continents have divided it unequally, for the threefold division indicates a division into three equal parts; but Libya lacks so much of being a third part of the inhabited world that even if it were combined with Europe, it would seem not to be equal to Asia. Perhaps it is even smaller than Europe; and in power it is much inferior.

The vision of the Earth supplied by Strabo is a striking departure from Herodotus, with Asia occupying more of the inhabited world than Europe and Libya combined. But most consequential is his claim about what such differences in size represent.

By connecting the small scale of Libya to its allegedly inferior power and drawing attention to its deserts and scattered settlements, he invites his readers to imagine that the size and character of a territory determine its political power.
3. Pliny on geography and empire

The connection between size and power is made even more explicit by the Roman naturalist Pliny the Elder in his Natural History (1st century CE). He offers a vision of the world reminiscent of Herodotus in which Europe is by far the largest of the continents:

To begin then with Europe, nurse of the race that has conquered all the nations, and by far the loveliest portion of the Earth, which most authorities, not without reason, have reckoned to be not a third part but a half of the world, dividing the whole circle into two portions by a line drawn from the river Don to the Straits of Gibraltar.
Later, he gives a more detailed account of these divisions, based on some confusing measurements drawn from several, sometimes conflicting, sources:

It is consequently clear that Europe is a little less than one and a half times the size of Asia, and two and one sixth times the width of Africa. Combining all these figures together, it will be clearly manifest that Europe is a little more than 1/3 + 1/8, Asia ¼ + 1/14, and Africa 1/5 + 1/60, of the whole Earth.

Pliny effectively inverts the point made by Strabo about the relationship between the small size of Libya and its lacklustre profile on the world stage and applies it to Europe. He situates his claim about the size of Europe right next to his celebration of it as the homeland of the Romans, who have become conquerors of the entire world. The juxtaposition suggests that the masters of the Earth fittingly occupy its greatest and most beautiful portion.
These episodes show us that, long before the debate over Mercator, the representation of the sizes of the continents was already entangled with questions about power and prestige.

The campaign for the Equal Earth Projection, and the proper recognition of the scale of Africa, proceeds from this same, ancient assumption: that the way a continent appears on the map can shape perceptions of its place in the world.

articles.title: Clarissa: this bold and emotional retelling moves Virginia Woolf’s Mrs Dalloway to modern-day Lagos
articles.author: Olumayokun Ogunde, PhD Candidate in English, City St George's, University of London
paras: In October I was sitting on a bench by the Thames, having just watched Clarissa at the BFI Southbank. It had been shown on the same screen where I once watched Mandabi (1968), the first feature-length film produced in west Africa. I thought to myself: here is a new version of African cinema.

Clarissa is written and directed by brothers Arie and Chuko Esiri. The film is a retelling of Virginia Woolf’s novel Mrs Dalloway (1925) that relocates the novel’s post-war London setting to contemporary Lagos, Nigeria.

It follows Clarissa (Sophie Okonedo) as she prepares to host a party and finds herself revisiting the choices that have shaped her life. The premise is familiar; Woolf’s story is now over 100 years old, but the film feels remarkably at home in its new setting. Lagos pours into every open space and fills the screen in much the same way that Woolf’s London fills the pages of her novel.

In an interview with Afrocritik, Chuko Esiri described the transposition as emerging naturally from his relationship with the book. He sees the novel’s themes manifesting in both Clarissa’s private reckoning with her life and the parallel story of Nigeria’s own history of independence, its great promise and the question of what has become of it.

“We all put our great futures behind us and settle,” Clarissa says. It is a line that belongs to the film’s particular meditation on ageing and the distance between the lives we imagined and the ones we inhabit. But it also speaks to the nation in which this story now unfolds. What does it mean to grow older, individually or collectively and to look back at the futures Nigerians once believed were theirs?
In Woolf’s novel, the London of 1923 is a city of imperial wealth and inherited privilege. The social world of the upper classes exists alongside the suffering of those it barely sees.

One of the book’s main characters, Peter Walsh, returns from India and finds London newly enchanting, its “civilisation” thrown into relief by comparison. The word carries the weight of an imperial worldview in which, inevitably, Britain is positioned as the measure against which other places are judged.

To transplant this story to Lagos is to unsettle that perspective. Instead of London, the film offers viewers the grandeur of Victoria Island (an affluent, upscale enclave in Lagos known for its wealth and luxury), the lushness of Clarissa’s home and the carefully managed elegance of her social circle. This, too, is a world of wealth and inherited status, a bubble in which guests can arrive at a party and ask whether there is food, only for Clarissa to assure them that “there are canapés floating around”.

This is not an owambe (a traditional lavish west African party). There is no great spread of rice, no amala woman (cook serving hot yam-flour swallow, a traditional, dough-like West African food) in the corner. The detail about the canapés is funny, but it also tells us something about the world these characters inhabit: a particular, cosmopolitan Lagos that draws on British social codes while remaining distinctly its own.

Elsewhere, the city is louder, more precarious, its rhythms spilling out of danfo buses (Lagos’s iconic yellow commercial minibuses) and into the lives of those beyond Clarissa’s circle. The film allows privilege and hardship to occupy the same city, as they do in reality.
Reading Woolf against herself

After watching Clarissa, I keep returning to Woolf’s language in her essay A Room of One’s Own, where she describes the supposed advantage of being a woman as being able to “pass even a very fine negress without wishing to make an Englishwoman of her”. The sentence exposes the limits of Woolf’s own racial imagination, the colonial gaze through which a Black woman can be observed without being granted the fullness of her personhood.
In the hands of a Nigerian filmmaker, this British literary classic acquires a different centre of gravity, one shaped by Black lives, desires and contradictions.

This is part of what makes Clarissa feel so assured in its retelling. In an interview, Okonedo describes the Esiri brothers as bold, singular in their vision and unburdened by the working-class insecurities that have shaped her own experience. There is something fitting about this confidence: a Nigerian film taking a story so deeply rooted in British literary culture and making it entirely its own, without asking permission or pausing to explain itself.

The joyful song Happy Day by Victor Uwaifo carries through the last moment with the characters as old friends dance together. These are people who have lived, who have made choices, who imagine they have left their great futures behind them. Yet there is joy here, too, and the possibility of being surprised by life again. Perhaps this is what retelling makes possible.

articles.title: Poems on the Underground at 40: how Shakespeare inspired one of London’s best-loved public art projects
articles.author: Ana Parejo Vadillo, Professor of English Literature and the Arts, Birkbeck, University of London
paras: If you have travelled on the London Underground at any time over the last 40 years, you’ll probably have noticed a poem or two. Perhaps on posters adorning the station concourse, or in tube carriages where adverts might normally be found.

These poems are often unexpected, delightful and poignant. They remind commuters of our humanness and offer travellers small moments of respite. Whether on an empty platform or in a crowded carriage, Londoners and tourists alike can be moved by the rhythms of poetry.

“I love dis great, polluted place,” says Benjamin Zephaniah in The London Breed (2001). “I sing of a world reshaped,” declares Nigerian poet Niyi Osundare with hope in I Sing of Change (1981). In A Bunch of Consolation (2023), Maura Dooley urges us “to love, to speak up, to hold steady”. A melancholic yearning for her mother’s cooking in Grace Nichols’ Like a Beacon (1984) – one of the first poems to be featured on a poster – beckons your appetite but breaks your heart.

This year Poems on the Underground has celebrated 40 years of bringing poetry to the commuting masses. The first poems to be displayed were Up in the Morning Early (1788) by Robert Burns; The Railway Children (1984) by Seamus Heaney; Like a Beacon (1984) by Grace Nichols; Ozymandias (1818) by Percy Bysshe Shelley; and This Is Just To Say (1934) by William Carlos Williams.

The project was the brainchild of the American essayist and novelist Judith Chernaik, who came up with the idea as a young academic when she moved to London in 1972 with her husband and children. The couple befriended the Barrow poets Gerard Benson and Cicely Herbert and soon became part of their literary circle. The Barrow poets were a group of writers and folk musicians who got their name from selling poems from handbarrows in local markets.

The couple were invited to attend play-reading groups, and in one such gathering, the work being explored was Shakespeare’s As You Like It. Chernaik was charmed by the figure of Orlando, who hangs poems in the trees of the Forest of Arden for his love, Rosalind.

Imagining the London Underground as a real-life contemporary Forest of Arden, she asked her friends what they thought of her idea to hang some poems in the advertising spaces on the tube. Delighted by the notion, they encouraged her, and the following morning, a determined Chernaik wrote to London Transport (later TfL).

To her amazement London Transport replied and was interested in her proposal. She secured an Arts Council Grant in 1985 and the rest is literary history: four decades of sharing poetry with the public though Poems on the Underground.

Literary academic Anna Barton has observed that in As You Like It, “the Forest of Arden is a place of freedom, transformation and love – but also hardship for the shepherds who work there”. But if Shakespeare was the inspiration for Chernaik, a scholar of Romantic poetry, the motivation came from her study of Percy Bysshe Shelley and John Keats.
Finding meaning amid the tumult

Keats, who died at just 26, worried in his letters whether he would be read, while Shelly believed poetry had the power to change the world. Here was a project that could accomplish both things. Indeed, joined by Gerard Benson and Cicley Herbert who became co-founders of the initiative, the three brought to millions of passengers a wide range of poetry from the past and present, and written by poets from all over the world.

Today Cherniak’s co-directors are the poets Imtiaz Dharker and George Szirtes; after the death of Benson in 2014, Herbert stepped back. The programme has been so successful it has been replicated in cities such as New York, Paris, Beijing, Dublin, Moscow, Shanghai and Warsaw.
In London, the tube rumbles to the rhythm of the best poetry in the world. One of my favourites is Oscar Wilde’s Symphony in Yellow, a poem first published in 1889.
An omnibus across the bridge
Crawls like a yellow butterfly,
And, here and there, a passer-by
Shows like a little restless midge.

When I first saw it on the tube, the poem transported me to the London of the 1890s. In the 19th century, omnibus routes were colour coded – how ingenious of Wilde to sing of the bus as a yellow butterfly. The design for the poem, which included an illustration depicting Oscar Wilde himself, made me aware of another aspect of the Poems on the Underground: their visual impact that comes from beautiful typography, use of colour and layout.

The poet Arthur Symons wrote in 1909 of the dehumanisation of passengers travelling on the Underground: “The creatures that we see now in the machines are hardly to be called human beings, so are they disfigured out of all recognition, in order that they may go fast enough not to see anything themselves.”

For the last 40 years, Poems on the Underground has done the exact opposite: it has continually reminded passengers of their humanity. And Symons would probably have been thrilled to know A Tune (1899), his poem about the persistence of memory, would one day be displayed on the tube.

Seamus Heaney, one of the first poets to be featured, wrote to Chernaik in 1999 to say: “I admire you for keeping the underground poems a priority; it is worth doing and has made a difference, I am sure, to the life-worth of poetry for many people. Blessings on the work.”

As the Poems on the Underground archive at the University of Cambridge attests, the project is much loved by the public and poets alike. It is a powerful example of the uplifting effect of the arts, and how bringing art into everyday public spaces can transform the experience of the people using them.

articles.title: Influencers are supposed to influence us – so why are they asking us what they should do?
articles.author: Catherine Greenwood, Lecturer in Digital Marketing, University of Lancashire
paras: An influencer posts a photograph of two designer handbags and asks her followers which one she should buy. Another wants recommendations for restaurants in a new city she is visiting. Someone else asks which beauty dupes are actually worth trying.

These are ordinary questions we might ask our friends. Yet, coming from people who have built careers influencing what others buy, wear and desire, they raise an interesting question. If influencers are supposed to influence their followers, why are they increasingly asking them what they should do? The answer may be that asking for advice may not mean giving up influence at all, but another way for influencers to maintain it.

In my doctoral research, I analysed 390 Instagram posts from three established luxury fashion influencers. I examined how they communicated identity, aspiration and authenticity through images, captions and other visual messaging.

One observation was the use of questions within captions, inviting followers to respond to content that was otherwise carefully constructed. A polished fashion photograph might be accompanied by conversational language, encouraging audiences to engage with the person behind the image.

These interactions interested me because they demonstrated how influencers could communicate exclusivity and accessibility simultaneously. They might be attending prestigious fashion events or wearing expensive clothing, yet their captions created opportunities for seemingly ordinary conversation.

No one’s 20s and 30s look the same. You might be saving for a mortgage or just struggling to pay rent. You could be swiping dating apps, or trying to understand childcare. No matter your current challenges, our Quarter Life series has articles to share in the group chat, or just to remind you that you’re not alone.
What’s your apocalypse skill? Finding a future‑proof hobby can bring fulfilment today
Five ways to enjoy fashion as a hobby without indulging in overconsumption
The ick: the psychology of why a romantic partner can suddenly repulse you

Asking followers for recommendations takes this a little further. There is a difference between asking people what they think of an outfit and inviting them to help make a decision. Followers are no longer simply responding to someone else’s taste, but being invited to contribute their own.

This is particularly interesting in fashion, where influence has traditionally been associated with possessing knowledge, recognising desirable things and communicating taste to others. Yet here we have people who possess considerable fashion authority apparently seeking that judgment from their audiences.
The performance of being approachable

In his influential book The Presentation of Self in Everyday Life (1959), sociologist Erving Goffman argued that people manage how they present themselves to others, adjusting their behaviour according to the impressions they wish to communicate.
This offers a useful way of understanding influencer culture, where seemingly informal moments can contribute to a carefully maintained public identity.

A homeware influencer might genuinely need advice about blinds. But asking also communicates something about them. It presents them as approachable, interested in other people’s experiences and willing to admit that they do not already know everything.
Importantly, none of these qualities requires an influencer to surrender the authority that made people follow them in the first place.

Media scholar Crystal Abidin describes this relationship through the concept of perceived interconnectedness. This describes the interactions that create a sense of familiarity and mutual connection between influencers and their audiences.

Unlike traditional celebrities, whose audiences largely watch from a distance, influencers operate within platforms that allow followers to speak back. Being asked for advice can deepen this sense of connection. There is a particular satisfaction in feeling that somebody whose life you follow might be interested in your opinion.
Who is actually influencing whom?

Of course, followers may genuinely shape an influencer’s decisions. Someone might recommend an unfamiliar designer, an independent restaurant or a product that subsequently appears in their content. It would be misleading to suggest that every question is a calculated attempt to generate engagement. But participation does not necessarily mean equal influence.

The influencer decides what to ask, which recommendations to acknowledge and whether to act on them. The audience may contribute the knowledge, but the influencer retains considerable control over how that knowledge is selected and presented.

This is where the blinds example is particularly interesting. The influencer’s followers might possess knowledge about suppliers, materials or products that she does not. Yet she retains the authority to decide what fits the aesthetic identity she has established. There is, after all, a difference between knowing where to buy something and knowing how to make it desirable.

When an influencer publicly adopts a follower’s recommendation, that choice can become influential in its own right. What began as somebody else’s advice becomes part of the influencer’s communication of taste.
This challenges the idea that influence simply travels in one direction. Instead, audiences can participate in producing the knowledge and cultural references that influencers subsequently share.

For fashion brands and marketers, this matters because an influencer’s value may lie not only in their ability to recommend products, but also in their ability to make audiences feel involved in the process through which recommendations acquire meaning.

Perhaps we have become so accustomed to influencers telling us what to buy that we overlook what happens when they ask us instead. The apparent reversal can make the relationship feel less hierarchical, without necessarily changing who holds the greatest authority.

articles.title: I’m an artist who works with glass – here’s how the physics and chemistry of glassblowing work
articles.author: Suzanne Peck, Lecturer of Art, Rochester Institute of Technology
paras: Glass as a material is full of contradictions. Depending on the form and use, glass can be fragile or strong, opaque or transparent, rough or smooth. The studios my colleagues and I teach and learn in, as glass instructors, echo this abundance of physical opposites. These environments are simultaneously immersive, complex, seductive and demanding.

When the studio is in action, you might hear glass breaking, hot metal being quenched in water, glassblowing pipes rolling on the workbench rails, and some good tunes on the stereo. You might smell hot beeswax and burning newspaper. You might feel a bit of waste glass under your shoe or the intense heat from the furnaces and a breeze from a well-placed fan. Glassblowers learn to listen, to feel and to find some focus within and among the kinetic.

The constant stimuli of the glass studio may not seem anything like a sterile science lab, and yet glass artists need to accrue knowledge of physics and chemistry to achieve any kind of control with this dynamic material. They must choose a material with the desired properties and during the process judge factors such as heat and malleability.

At Rochester Institute of Technology, where I help run the glass program, we primarily use two types of glasses. In our hot glass studio we melt “soft” glass. This glass is specifically formulated to be melted in a furnace and used by the glassblower. It’s a combination of fine mesh silica sand, soda ash and lime, with small amounts of a few additional ingredients that keep the glass beautiful when it’s at its top temperature of 2,200 degrees Fahrenheit (1,204 degrees Celsius).

In our flameworking studio, we use a borosilicate glass. You might recognize this glass as the brand Pyrex made in Corning, New York. This is a super heat-resistant glass. It melts at a higher temperature than soft glass and arrives to our students in preformed rods that they can melt and shape by torch in our flameworking studio. The differences in chemistry really change how these glasses look and behave.

Glass, from a material science perspective, is categorized as an amorphous solid, meaning that glass’s molecules are arranged in a near-random pattern and there is no sharp melting point. Rather, glass gradually softens over a wide temperature range.
Once you’ve adjusted to the chaos of the studio, it’s time to start working.

We have two furnaces in our hot glass studio, where we work with soft glass, so anytime during the school year there is between 700 to 1,200 pounds of glass. It’s kept in the furnace at its molten state (2,200 degrees F or 1,204 degrees C), ready to be gathered and transformed.

When we work with the material, transforming it with tools and breath and heat, it needs to be kept in a workable heat zone – probably between 1,100 and 2,000 F (593 and 1,094 C). When the glass dips below that range, we perceive it as solid, though at the molecular level it is still dynamic and acting more like a liquid.

To make anything – a sculpture, a tumbler, a celestial magical orb or a pumpkin – you start by gathering glass out of the furnace on a metal rod. Once you’ve gathered your glass, you start making decisions.

You might ask yourself: What tools do I need to begin to shape and transform this glass into the object I have in mind? If you wait too long and the glass begins cooling down, you’ll need to reheat it to reintroduce malleability, allowing you to continue working it without breaking it.

A big part of glasswork is moving between the reheating chamber and the bench, where the artist uses tools to move and stretch the molten glass into the desired shape. You’ll need to alternate between these two stations many times.

Glassblowing is a team activity. I have physical and intellectual support from my colleagues: breath from their lungs, protection from the heat, additional bits of glass brought from the furnace to add to my object. We almost never work alone.

So, say I want to make a very basic clear tumbler. This is a simple conceptual object – utilitarian, domestic and intimate. It is also a tricky one to make well: too heavy and it feels bad in the hand, too thick at the lip and it dribbles when you drink, too thin at the bottom and it will break before it is complete.

Maybe I want to design it so it is slightly conical: wider at the bottom than the top, so it’s less likely to tip over. Maybe I want it to have a little indent for the user’s thumb as a gentle invitation to her hand. First I make my design: I draw it. I share it with my team so they can predict the process and the object’s needs. Then we begin.

I gather glass out of the furnace, let it cool a bit, then introduce a bubble in the glass by blowing into the pipe, the hollow rod that attaches to the object I’m making. I reheat, sit at the bench and begin to shape the glass using both gravity and the Jills, a cooling and shaping tool. The Jills is kind of like a large pair of tongs. It hasn’t changed much in design for 2,000 years.

I ask for some air from my teammate, and she blows into the pipe while I’m shaping the glass. The bubble transforms into a pill shape, slightly wider at the bottom. I constrict the area right in front of the pipe. I’m focusing on shape and heat, taking care to not let the glass get too cold. If the glass drops to about 1,000 F (538 C), it enters a danger zone. If it’s not yet finished, it needs to be warmed up in the reheating chamber; or if it is done, put away in a kiln to cool slowly.

If glass cools too quickly, the molecules freeze into a chaotic pattern, which causes stresses that result in fracture. To combat this volatility, when the glass object is done and ready to be cooled, we place the object in an annealer: a kiln set to a resting temperature of 930 F (500 C).

This temperature is like a Goldilocks zone for our glass: It’s not so hot that the glass will deform, but not so cool that the glass will stress and break. Once the kilns are full, a computer guide takes them down to room temperature over about 10 hours.

As I continue to work on my cup, I get more heat, focusing on the very end of the bubble – the part that will be the base of the cup. I then sit down and have another member of my team flatten the bottom with a wooden paddle while I tool the glass with the Jills to keep its shape. The cycle continues on and on.

The process is quick, but also there are so many little steps that it would take nearly a full-length book to describe them all. When asked how long it takes to make a tumbler, I’ll often answer, “About 10 years or 10 minutes, depending on how you think about time and material knowledge.” This is both glib and true. Glass demands attention, dedication and a willingness to make connections between physics and chemistry and your observable experiences. It is a highly challenging and equally rewarding material to work with and alongside. I count myself very lucky.

articles.title: Centuries before TikTok, this 1579 bestseller gave readers their daily dose of ‘brain rot’
articles.author: James Fox, Research Associate in the School of Modern Languages and Cultures, University of Glasgow
paras: First you are shown a new hack to keep wine from spoiling. Then a dog lovingly devoted to its owner. Immediately in tow there are methods to repair broken glass and remove acne, a tip for weight loss, a cake recipe and an astrological reading of your future. But this is not your TikTok or Instagram feed – it’s the contents of a book written nearly four-and-a-half centuries ago.

The English writer Thomas Lupton’s book A Thousand Notable Things was first published in 1579. True to its title, it collected roughly 1,000 short passages ordered randomly, one after another. A seemingly endless stream of household “life hacks”, sensational stories and recipes, it offered answers for just about everything.

Trouble sleeping? Rub your forehead with a mix of white poppy and henbane seeds. If you find yourself bewitched, leave a mercury-filled quill under your pillow. And have you heard the folklore that claims when a robin red breast finds a dead human, they cover its face in moss?

Flitting through eclectic, attention-grabbing short-form content may be the de facto mode of media consumption in the 21st century. But how-to books like A Thousand Notable Things suggest that our ancestors’ preoccupations were not entirely different.

Lupton understood the wide appeal of such easily digestible material. In a revealing preface, he argued that imbibing many passages of “strangeness and variety” was preferable to being “fed too long with one food” by reading entire books.

It proved a winning formula. A Thousand Notable Things enjoyed at least 33 editions, remaining in print from the time Sir Francis Drake was circumnavigating the globe until 1827, the year the first known photograph was taken.
Its success belonged to a burgeoning taste for “books of secrets”, recipe-like instructional texts that taught everything from cosmetics and alchemy to brewing and beekeeping.

Originating in Italy, and published throughout the 16th, 17th and 18th centuries, the most popular of these works were continually translated and reprinted throughout Europe. They are now recognised as exerting genuine influence on contemporary scientific culture.

Whether providing alchemical routes to the philosopher’s stone or the recipe for a nutritious stew, books like A Thousand Notable Things thrived on the promise of revealing hidden “secrets” about nature’s inner workings.

Of course, there was no guarantee that everything Lupton suggested would work: whether sleeping on your right side during pregnancy really meant the baby would be female, or that dreaming of eagles flying overhead was necessarily a sign of imminent good fortune. Sheer efficacy alone wasn’t the point. The appeal lay in the wonder, curiosity and amusement that accompanied practical instruction.

If some passages sound absurd or downright dangerous to modern ears (henbane and mercury are highly poisonous), consider that much of Lupton’s material was cutting-edge in its day. His most cited source was Antoine Mizauld, a Parisian medical professor and advisor to French queen Marguerite de Valois.
Even though the vitality of astrology, occult science and ancient medicine waned over the book’s 250-year lifespan, the deeply human concerns it addressed proved enduringly popular.
We know that contemporary readers found Lupton’s eclectic material engaging thanks to their annotations in personal copies, precious few of which remain today.

One survivor from 1612, now in the Glasgow University Library, is marked with small crosses at passages on lameness, heart trouble, ulcers, meat eating and stomach problems. We might speculate that its owner was managing symptoms of dietary issues or gout. So too are gout cures underlined in a copy owned by the 17th-century book collector Frances Wolfreston.
Another reader pencilled crosses next to 38 predominantly medical passages in their 1706 copy, including remedies for head and toothaches, burning eyes, shortness of breath, sore throat and insomnia.

Others were more selective. One copy in the Wellcome Collection is marked only occasionally, including at an anecdote about a German farmer who died with terrible pain in his side. A surgeon cut him open to find large pieces of wood and four steel knives, afflictions that were blamed on the Devil.

Just as we worry today about the pernicious effects of TikTok, 16th-century commentators also feared the “brain-rotting” potential of low-brow mass entertainment, distraction and information overload.

But Lupton’s take was more optimistic. Offering bite-size morsels gleaned from a wide range of texts, in plain English rather than scholarly Latin, gave ordinary readers access to knowledge that otherwise required whole libraries to attain.

These how to books, which are the subject of an ongoing research collaboration between Glasgow University and the Herzog August library in Germany, will take centre stage in an exhibition at the Mitchell Library, Glasgow, from January to March 2027.

Whether or not they are direct antecedents of today’s instructional media, these texts encapsulate both the past’s profound strangeness, and those facets of human experience that seem perennial: the potent dialectic of similarity and difference that makes history so compelling. If nothing else, they might provide a handy hack to stave off your next headache.

articles.title: Ernest Shackleton turned a major disappointment in the Antarctic into fame back in Britain
articles.author: Ed Armston-Sheret, Fellow at the Institute of Historical Research, School of Advanced Study, University of London
paras: Ernest Shackleton is one of the most well-known polar explorers in history. He’s mostly remembered for his incredible leadership following the sinking of his ship Endurance in the Weddell Sea in November 1915, which saved his life and the 27 others on board.

Yet had you known Shackleton in 1895, his future fame as an Antarctic explorer would have seemed highly unlikely. At the time, he was an unknown officer in the merchant navy, and Antarctica meant little to him. He had never even put on a pair of skis.

So how did Shackleton become such a famous polar explorer? This is one of the questions at the heart of my book The Grip of the Ice and the answer is suprising: his fame had as much to do with what he did back home as it did with his time on the ice.

Shackleton’s polar career started with the British National Antarctic Expedition, usually known as the Discovery Expedition (named after its ship). The venture was jointly organised by the Royal Geographical Society and the Royal Society and partly funded by the government. The gregarious Shackleton found a place on the expedition by befriending Cedric Longstaff, the son of one of the expedition’s major donors. On the March 15 1901, Shackleton was ordered to report to the Discovery’s commander, Robert Falcon Scott, at the expedition’s office in Mayfair. He would be the ship’s third lieutenant.

Arriving in Antarctica in January 1902, they explored the continent’s coast and then spent the winter on board their ship in McMurdo Sound. During the months of polar darkness, conditions were too harsh for further exploration. Shackleton became a vital and well-liked member of the Discovery expedition. To help keep up morale while cooped up on board the ship, he edited The South Polar Times – the first magazine ever published in Antarctica.

Shackleton soon heard exciting news: Scott had selected him, along with the expedition’s zoologist and junior medic Edward Wilson, to accompany him on a journey towards the South Pole. This would be the expedition’s first major journey.

Leaving the ship on November 2 1902, the journey started off well, with Siberian huskies helping to pull the men’s sledges. They were soon further south than any explorers before them. But things gradually began to unravel. The dogs weakened due to problems with their food, the men grew hungry on insufficient supplies and they couldn’t move their sledges forward all st once, drastically reducing their daily distances.

Shackleton and Scott may also have had an argument on this journey, with Albert Armitage, the expedition’s second in command, later suggesting in his letters that Scott called Shackleton a “bloody fool” during a heated argument. Even so, they patched things up and trudged southwards. Eventually, they managed to lighten their sledges by leaving supplies for the return march in a depot, improving their rate of progress. However, their dogs continued to weaken so Shackleton and Wilson killed the sickest animals and fed them to the stronger ones.

By Christmas 1902, the men were also in trouble. Wilson inspected the men’s gums and noticed signs of scurvy – a disease we now know is caused by a lack of vitamin C. Soon, they were forced to turn back, having achieved a new furthest south record of around 480 miles from the South Pole on December 31 1902.

On the march back to the ship, Shackleton’s health deteriorated rapidly. As well as suffering from scurvy, he was also coughing up blood. When the last of their dogs was killed, Scott and Wilson pulled the sledge while Shackleton made painful progress on skis.
Eventually, on February 3 1903, they got back to the ship to find that the Morning, a relief vessel, had arrived.

The Discovery was still trapped in the ice and, with winter closing in, Scott ordered that Shackleton return to New Zealand when the Morning sailed northwards on March 2 1903. Among polar historians, Scott’s decision has been controversial. Some suggest that Scott saw Shackleton as a potential rival, though there isn’t a great deal of evidence for this.
Early return and celebrity

So, Shackleton’s career as a polar explorer seemed to have got off to a bad start. While Scott sent him back with a glowing reference, he had been pronounced unfit for further Antarctic exploration. Frustratingly, he seemed “practically well” according to Gerald S Doorly, then a junior officer on the Morning, by the time he arrived in New Zealand and was in even better shape when he reached London.
Shackleton’s diaries show that he felt a mix of emotions: frustration, embarrassment and disappointment. He had been desperate to stay another winter and see the expedition through to its finish.
Yet studying this period, what amazed me was how Shackleton took advantage of his early return to Britain.

As the only officer back from Antarctica, he was in a unique position to tell the public and the media what had happened on their journey. He wrote articles for The Illustrated London News and Pearson’s Magazine and gave lectures to enthralled audiences, eager to hear about his amazing journey towards the South Pole.

Shackleton was also involved in equipping a relief vessel, the Dundee whaler Terra Nova, to help free the explorers from the ice the following year. By early 1904, he’d even managed to land a job as secretary of the Royal Scottish Geographical Society.

The Discovery expedition transformed Shackleton from an unknown officer in the Merchant Navy into one of the best-known polar explorers in Britain. He’d also built a wealth of logistical experience and connections that left him perfectly placed to launch an expedition of his own – which he did in 1907, much to Scott’s annoyance.
In his return to London, Shackleton had demonstrated his unique ability to make the very best of a disaster.

articles.title: Archaeological finds at an Irish fort reveal insights into the finer side of medieval life
articles.author: Michelle Comber, Lecturer in Archaeology, School of Geography, Archaeology and Irish Studies, University of Galway
paras: Popular media, from computer games to movies, often portrays medieval life as being dominated by fighters and farmers. In these depictions, there’s little evidence of a world beyond political struggle and simple subsistence.

Leisure activities are often overlooked, despite the fact that they existed in one form or another at most – if not all – levels of medieval society. The intangible nature of much of the evidence, often coupled with poor preservation of physical objects, can help explain this.

However, when conditions are right, archaeological remains can shed light on the extra-curricular activities of medieval folk. My colleagues and I found abundant evidence of life’s luxuries at the site of Caherconnell Cashel in the Burren region of western Ireland.

Caherconnell Cashel was a farmstead of houses and workshops enclosed within a well-preserved circular dry stone wall. Such settlements are also known as ringforts and generally housed a single family (possibly multiple generations). Caherconnell was a large ringfort; the home of wealthy local rulers from the late 10th century AD to the early 17th century. Our recently concluded excavations revealed all aspects of life at this well-preserved family settlement.

While activities such as fighting, farming, industry and crafts were clearly represented in material recovered from the site, so too were the less mundane activities of game playing, literacy, and music.

The true extent of game playing is undoubtedly lost in the perishable nature of the materials used extensively in such pursuits – such as wood, leather and textiles. At Caherconnell, however, surviving evidence includes small gaming pieces made of bone and antler, metal, clay and stone.

One of the more complete finds was an 11th-century barrel-shaped and polished antler gaming piece. A bronze peg or stem runs through its hollow core and projects from its base. It originally had a plate or cap at the top, the loss of which may have resulted in the piece being discarded or set aside for repair.

Pegged game pieces like this were used in the Saxon and Viking board game of hnefatafl, a game that appeared in Ireland around the 9th or 10th century AD. Hnefatafl, and other games like it, provided both strategy training and entertainment.

Evidence of literacy at Caherconnell includes writing implements and associated equipment. One of our most remarkable finds was an 11th-century pen made from bone and bronze. The slender hollow bone shaft or barrel was probably made from the bone of a wader bird or swan.

Experimental work by the archaeologist Adam Parsons found that the closest match was a swan radius (a tubular bone) from the right-side wing. Inserted into the narrow end of the barrel is a tapering bronze point or nib.

The Caherconnell pen finds no exact comparisons within Ireland or elsewhere; its early secular context is also, so far, unique. Until now, evidence of early literacy in Ireland has been largely confined to monastic and related church sites. At Caherconnell, the pen may have been used in general record keeping and external communications.

However, it also reminds us that literate occupants of Caherconnell Cashel may have enjoyed composing, reading, and sharing ancestral pedigrees, praise poetry and epic tales “of gods and fighting men”.
The musical sounds of a settlement are rarely represented in its archaeological record. Wood, a common material in the construction of various instruments, rarely survives to the present day.

Metal and bone fittings, however, have been found during excavations, including at Caherconnell, where bone and bronze tuning pegs were among the finds. Two of the tuning pegs are readily identifiable as components of stringed instruments.

They have a circular sectioned shaft that splays slightly into a rectangular sectioned turning block at one end (now missing from the larger bone example). The opposite end pinches in slightly and is perforated by a small circular hole through which the string was attached.
The bone tuning peg, being a relatively soft material, still bears impressions from the wire-string of the instrument. Both date to the 11th century, but they are clearly from different instruments.
One had strong bronze pegs, the other had larger bone versions. Outside Ireland, shorter tuning pegs are commonly associated with lyres, lutes and fiddles (up to 65mm is classed as short).

No lutes or fiddles survive from early Ireland, however. Nor are there any written references to, or depictions of them. The lyre, on the other hand, is represented. Depictions are found in several ecclesiastical contexts and early Irish literature confirms that lyres or lyre-like instruments were also used outside religious settings.

Music, and accompanying songs and poetry, probably fulfilled various social, political, and cultural functions. These range from proclaiming the magnificence of the nobility to entertaining a family around their hearth in the evening.

Life at Caherconnell was, in many ways, very traditional. It was a place where ancestry and heritage were valued, yet it was also a place connected to the outside world. In leisure, as in so many other facets of their lives, the occupants encountered, adopted, and no doubt adapted the most desirable elements of a wider cultural realm.

It is clear from this one site that those with more leisure time, often the wealthier in society, filled that time with various recreational pursuits. However, human nature suggests that all classes engaged in such activities, albeit often in a manner that’s less visible to archaeologists.

After all, you didn’t need a fancy bronze and antler game set to play games, writing equipment to create stories, or peg-tuned wired instruments to compose and sing a song. Such things just prove the existence of these activities, not how commonplace they were.
